comparison: Perfect agreement on model architecture claims (C24, C26-C28, C95-C96). Both evaluations find the modeling approach clear, well-reasoned, and appropriately transparent about limitations. OpenEval notes lack of quantitative regime boundaries as minor weakness; peer reviewers explicitly praise clarity and explicitness.

Strong agreement on model behavior across parameter space (C29-C36). Both find the three-regime characterization well-supported by Figure 2. Peer reviewers also include C3-C4 in this evaluation, treating the intermediate regime identification as a central, mechanistically-grounded contribution. OpenEval notes missing quantitative thresholds; peer reviewers describe evidence as 'convincing.'

Strong agreement on convergent peaks across metrics (C41-C48). Both evaluations treat this as a key theoretical contribution unifying perturbational and spontaneous complexity. OpenEval appropriately notes sparse direct evidence for fluidity-attractor link (C42) and temporal window discrepancy (C90); peer reviewers accept findings without challenging these acknowledged limitations.

Perfect agreement on empirical heterogeneity findings (C56-C63). Both evaluations accept the variable performance across metrics and drugs, with OpenEval explicitly praising transparency about reversed patterns and overlapping distributions. Peer reviewers describe evidence as 'convincing' despite inconsistencies, treating variability as honest data reporting rather than methodological flaw.

Agreement on empirical dataset validity (C49-C52). Both evaluations accept the Sarasso et al. dataset and methodology without criticism. Peer reviewers also include C53-C54 (PCI benchmarks) in their evaluation. OpenEval notes small sample size as limitation; peer reviewers treat dataset as methodologically sound for proof-of-concept.

Agreement on PCI benchmark validity (C53-C54). Both evaluations accept established PCI benchmarks as appropriate gold standard. OpenEval cites Casarotto et al. 2016 and Figure 5; peer reviewers incorporate this into broader acceptance of validation approach without specific critique.

Agreement on functional repertoire's robust performance (C64-C65). Both evaluations find complete separation across all subjects strongly supported by Figure 4b. OpenEval notes apparent contradiction with C93 regarding group-level predictive power; peer reviewers accept findings without addressing this inconsistency.

Agreement on classification results (C66-C70). Both evaluations accept complementary performance of fluidity vs. functional repertoire. OpenEval notes lack of cross-validation and statistical testing as limitation; peer reviewers describe evidence as 'convincing' and accept the unified framework without methodological concerns.

Agreement on main conclusions (C71-C72). Both evaluations support the core findings linking model predictions to empirical validation. OpenEval notes indirect connection due to generic connectome and timescale differences; peer reviewers explicitly endorse mechanistic basis and practical advantages, treating conclusions as well-established.

Strong agreement on theoretical framework (C73-C80). Both evaluations accept the literature-based theoretical grounding without objection. OpenEval notes appropriate hedging on criticality debate (C77, C80); peer reviewers implicitly endorse framework by noting broad interdisciplinary relevance.

Agreement on study motivation (C1-C2). Both evaluations accept background claims about PCI importance and TMS-EEG limitations. Peer reviewers also include C13-C16 in their evaluation. OpenEval notes C9's accessibility claim lacks direct comparison; peer reviewers treat motivation as addressing 'classic research' without challenge.

Disagreement on Ketamine classification claim (C88). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting Figure 4 contradicts the claim that metrics consistently distinguish Ketamine. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the finding and treating acknowledged limitations as appropriate scientific discussion rather than fundamental flaw.

Agreement on limitations and future directions (C92-C94). Both evaluations accept these as appropriate acknowledgments. OpenEval notes apparent inconsistency in C93 regarding functional repertoire's group-level power; peer reviewers accept limitations without addressing this specific inconsistency.

Agreement on theoretical interpretation (C83-C85). Both evaluations accept the interpretation of modeling results. OpenEval notes C84's claim about fluidity capturing 'number of attractors' is speculative (acknowledged in C42); peer reviewers endorse the unified framework without challenging speculative elements.

OpenEval evaluates C39 (low sPCI in extreme regimes) as SUPPORTED based on Figure 3 and Figure 2 supplement 1. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this claim about bistable dynamics in extreme coupling regimes.

OpenEval rates C89-C91 (temporal window discrepancy) as UNCERTAIN, noting the 20-fold difference between sPCI and PCI windows is asserted but not rigorously demonstrated through sensitivity analysis. Peer reviewers do not specifically address this methodological concern.

Agreement on literature background (C10-C23). OpenEval finds all background claims appropriately cited and consistent with established knowledge. Peer reviewers address subset (C13-C16) as part of broader acceptance of study motivation and theoretical grounding.

OpenEval evaluates C86-C87 (prior work citations) as SUPPORTED, noting appropriate contextualization with Hudetz et al. 2016 and Colombo et al. 2019. Peer reviewers do not specifically address these citation claims.
